problem: The 'feed and final' series joins (60 °C, 40 g/100 g water) straight to (20 °C, 20 g/100 g water). Both end points already lie on the solubility line, so this drawn 'cooling path' sits exactly on top of the curve and tells the student nothing. More seriously, it is the wrong path: while the solution cools with no crystals forming, its concentration stays at 40 g/100 g water, so the composition moves horizontally at C = 40 from 60 °C to 20 °C. The point (20 °C, 40 g/100 g water) is the supersaturated state, well above the curve at 20 g/100 g water, and only then does the mother liquor settle back to (20, 20) as crystals form.
fix: Caption: 'Solubility against temperature. A saturated solution at 60 °C (40 g per 100 g water) cooled without crystallising stays at 40 g per 100 g water and moves horizontally to 20 °C, ending above the curve — that is the supersaturated state. Crystallisation then brings the mother liquor back to the curve at 20 g per 100 g water.' Change the second series points to [[60, 40], [20, 40]] and keep the final point (20, 20) as a separate marker.

problem: The physics is right (C* falls while C stays), but the pointer 'This is the straight line in the figure' is wrong: a line at constant C is horizontal, while the figure shows a slanted line falling from 40 to 20.
fix: Write: 'Cooling: C* falls while C stays, so S rises. On the figure this is a horizontal move leftwards at constant concentration, taking the solution above the curve.'

problem: The formula crystals = W(C₁ − C₂)/100 and the words 'C₁ is the solubility at the feed temperature' hold only when the feed is saturated. If the feed is unsaturated, C₁ must be the actual solute concentration in the feed per 100 g water, otherwise the crystals are overstated.
fix: State the condition: 'valid when the feed is saturated at the feed temperature; for an unsaturated feed use the actual feed concentration in place of C₁'.
